#707. Documentary ‘Porno Para Ricardo,’ About Cuban Punk Musician Gorki, Shows ‘the Struggle of a Free Spirit Trapped in a Cage’

When Czech documentarian and photographer Hana Jakrlová encountered the crumbling streets of Cuba after meeting the dissident punk musician Gorki there, she had a strangely familiar sensation.

“I was living in New York at the time,” she recalls, “and Obama had just begun the process of warming relations with Cuba. All my friends in New York were worried about Cuba changing and McDonald’s popping up on every corner.” Related Stories ‘Drummer Boy’ Review: Love, Family and Revolution Conflict at Musket’s Point in a Swoony Period Musical

“So I went to photograph Cuba – and experienced the strangest sense of déjà vu. I had spent the first 20 years of my life in communist Czechoslovakia, and being in Cuba felt like stepping back into my youth, only in a Caribbean setting. Everything was familiar: the hopelessness, the absurdity, the propaganda, the misery – both economic and, above all, spiritual.”

Then, she says, she met a Cuban punk guitar player and leader of the banned group Porno para Ricardo, leading to a 12-year production journey that culminated this week in her feature docu debut, “Porno Para Ricardo,” which screened recently at the Ji.hlava International Documentary Film Festival.

“After talking to him and attending a Porno para Ricardo rehearsal (at Gorki’s house – the band had been completely driven underground by the Cuban regime and could no longer perform in public), I realized I wanted to make a project about this guy.”

At first as part of Jakrlová’s photography project on Cuban anti-regime artists, she soon realized she needed to concentrate on Gorki and his band, she says.

“I also came to understand that something was missing from my photographs of a punk band. So I started filming, initially with my own camera and later with a director of photography.”

That was in 2014, the director says, adding she’s now been to Cuba 10 times and spent almost a year there in total. “One thing that has always remained a mystery to me is how the establishment kept letting me back in.”

Jakrlová sometimes filmed herself and also used archival material “shot by the brilliant Cuban documentary filmmaker and dissident Claudio Fuentes.”

But she brought in respected Czech cinematographer Adam Ol’ha to help capture the remarkably striking visuals of Gorki’s life and struggles.

“We also worked with local talent – sound people and others – and some of them faced serious repercussions for their courage in working with us.”

“I wanted to show the struggle of a free spirit trapped in a cage,” Jakrlová says. “The life of an artist and dissident who has dedicated his entire life to fighting a totalitarian regime, spent three years in prison and faces persecution and oppression on a daily basis. But I also wanted to show a man torn between his love for his country and his love for his family. Gorki has a five-year-old grandson who lives in exile with his daughter, and Gorki has never been able to see him.”

Then, things changed, thanks to Cuban authorities, she says. “The regime gave him a clear ultimatum: Either he leaves the country or he goes to prison.”

“So, after filming Gorki’s dramatic departure into forced exile, the film became not only a punk essay on freedom, but also a film about exile.”

Filming her subject in Cuba involved daily harassment and threats from police, Jakrlová says. They also worried about another possibility: That he could die in a mysterious car accident, as has happened to several Cuban dissidents.”

The regime worries about its image abroad, says Jakrlová. “This helps explain why our crew wasn’t arrested during the shoot. However, we were followed constantly, as became apparent during Gorki’s subsequent arrest.”

As for why Gorki has always remained so passionate about his message (“This is for the bitch Raul Castro,” he yells while introducing one anti-regime song) Jakrlová says she came to understand they share some core beliefs.

“We are both freedom-loving people. Unlike Gorki, I was lucky enough to see communism fall in my country towards the end of my adolescence, so I never had to find out whether I had it in me to fight against it. What motivates Gorki is his love of freedom, his need for freedom, and also his sense of responsibility.”

“And that’s what connects Gorki with people like Václav Havel, Oswaldo Payá or Nelson Mandela. These were courageous and truly inspirational people. I feel incredibly lucky to have met two of them: Gorki Águila and Václav Havel.”

Jakrlová’s greatest challenge in completing “Porno Para Ricardo,” she says, was the deep daily dysfunction of Cuban society.

“Being a director is challenging, especially in a country where nothing works and nobody expects anything to work.”

“The only thing that worked 100% was Gorki. He is the most responsible person I know, always ready to work. He even risked his life by waiting for the film crew to arrive in Cuba after the regime had threatened him and given him an ultimatum: Leave his country or go to prison.”

Gorki now resides in Mexico, where he is awaiting a decision on a U.S. visa that would reunite him with his wife, daughter and grandson in Florida, Jakrlová says.

#706. ‘GTA VI’ Industry Domination Will Not End Anytime Soon

Without even having a PC launch date or a 'Grand Theft Auto Online' announcement, Rockstar Games has sold more than 17 million copies of its (latest) masterpiece.

If you’re just waking up from a coma, we’ve got good news. If you’ve been in the coma since 2013, we’ve got really good news.

After 13 years and what has felt like as many delays, Grand Theft Auto VI comes out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at midnight (your local time). Finally. Pre-launch, GTA VI is already a smash hit, approaching $1.7 billion in pre-sales (and more than 17 million units sold), according to Sensor Tower data. It is also getting perfect review scores.

Probably no single piece of media has been as highly anticipated as GTA VI, developed and published by Take-Two Interactive imprint Rockstar Games. Some of the excitement is measurable. Last week, GTA VI ranked number one on Screen Engine/ASI’s “Global Attention Share” chart, claiming 5.64 percent of the pie and booting Minecraft out of the spot it held for 45 straight weeks. It was the first time an unreleased game reach first place. Actually, it was the first time an unreleased game ranked better than fourth place (2019’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare).

GTA VI has now spent 15 weeks in the international research firm’s global top 10, obliterating Modern Warfare‘s record of three weeks. (Screen Engine/ASI balances Google search volume, Twitch and YouTube traffic, and Steam activity to arrive at a proprietary percentage of attention across thousands of games; tracking began in 2019.)

Colan Neese, Screen Engine/ASI’s senior vice president of gaming, tells The Hollywood Reporter he expects GTA VI‘s Global Attention Share will exceed 10 percent when the current week’s numbers come out on Tuesday, Nov. 24. Neese predicts GTA VI will occupy his top spot through at least January 2027.

Gene Park, the digital culture and video games critic for The Washington Post, has already beaten Grand Theft Auto VI. It took him 55 hours of gameplay. (Park and select other reviewers received preview codes — and serious NDAs — from Rockstar.)

But there is so much more for Park in the seemingly endless playground that is Vice City: GTA VI‘s setting based on real-life Miami. Park has since tacked on another 115 hours of gameplay, and is in no way bored.

When we spoke on Wednesday, Park was in the middle of a second full run through the game. This time, he is deliberately making different choices for the protagonists Jason and Lucia. The diverse results, Park says, have been staggering. (Also, he just discovered a zoo after 170 hours of gameplay — that should give you a sense of GTA VI‘s sheer scale.)

There are “just two ways” GTA VI “could have disappointed,” Joost van Dreunen, a video-game industry strategist and NYU professor, told THR. The first would have taken “some kind of awful geopolitical event.” Boy does it feel like we came close during this past week. The second is series of crippling bugs a la Cyberpunk 2077. Rockstar would have never let that happen, van Dreunen said. The publisher would have just delayed GTA VI a third time.

As it is, GTA VI is awesome. After a baker’s-dozen years and an $80-$100 price tag, it had to be. The anticipation (and those delays) has created a “novel… simultaneous synchronized event” experience for a single-player video game, van Dreunen said, which was not possible prior to the digital age. (Rockstar is not releasing GTA VI discs.)

Park believes it will be “a couple of months at the very least” before we get an Online option. GTA V‘s Online component still brings in $300-$500 million per year in revenue, per van Dreunen, through Shark Cash Cards. (You pay real money for in-game currency; Grand Theft Auto Online launched just two weeks after GTA V.)

Van Dreunen says GTA VI will be the dominant video game for “easily” a year, and probably longer. Its coming (but not announced) PC launch and inevitable GTA Online integration (also not announced) will keep the champagne corks popping like, well, Rockstar’s parent company’s stock. Shares of Take-Two Interactive’s Software (TTWO) are up more than 7 percent (from Tuesday’s market close) on those glowing GTA VI reviews — and Wednesday was a down day for the major index funds.

GTA VI officially releases on Thursday. Completely unrelated, boss, I feel a cold coming on…

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks."

Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#701. Fears of rising antisemitism in Europe

Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny commemorates the victims of Auschwitz as Jewish communities across Europe face growing hostility. What does the promise of "Never Again" mean for Jewish life in Europe today?

Regina Sluszny makes her way in her wheelchair through the iron gate marking the entrance to the former Auschwitz concentration camp. "I feel the cold, both physically and emotionally," says the 87-year-old Jewish woman, her gaze fixed on the grey horizon.

How many times has she been here? Six, seven, perhaps eight, she estimates. And each time, the same thoughts run through her mind: "I think about my husband's family. He lost seven loved ones here. They were sent straight to the gas chambers and murdered."

Regina Sluszny traveled to Poland with a delegation from the European Jewish Association (EJA), a European advocacy group representing Jewish interests that regularly organizes conferences on Jewish life as well as visits to former concentration camps.

This year, the organization invited political representatives and members of Jewish communities to Krakow and Auschwitz on November 9 and 10. The trip was deliberately scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the November Pogroms of 1938, widely regarded as a watershed moment on the path to the Holocaust.

"Honoring the past, securing the future" is the event's motto. Like many others in attendance, Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny fears that the horrors of the Shoah are slowly fading from Europe's collective memory.

Among this year's international religious and political representatives, the guest of honor was Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah and a prominent opponent of the Islamic Republic. The European Jewish Association (EJA) honored him for his efforts to combat antisemitism.

Accepting the award, Pahlavi recalled the historic ties between the Persian and Jewish peoples and called on democratic nations around the world to unite against oppression and ideological extremism.

But talking to attendees at the symposium in Krakow, it quickly becomes clear that fear of rising antisemitism is much closer to home. Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe.

In France, authorities recorded a total of 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025. That was fewer than in 2024, but around three times as many as in 2022.

In Germany, the number of antisemitic crimes recorded by police rose from 2,641 in 2022 to 6,236 in 2024 and 6,548 in 2025. Authorities and monitoring organizations across Europe have reported a significant increase in antisemitic incidents since October 7, 2023.

For Ellen van Praagh, chair of the Interprovincial Rabbinate in the Netherlands, October 7, 2023, marked a turning point. She also lost a family member during the Hamas-led attack which saw around 1,200 people in Israel killed and over 250 taken hostage and abducted to the Gaza Strip.

"My family has lived in the Netherlands since the 16th century. And now I'm being told to leave," says van Praagh. She says the atmosphere in the Netherlands has changed dramatically since the attack. She no longer feels safe there as a Jew. "We Jews are being held responsible for Israel's actions."

Israel launched a major military offensive in the Gaza Strip after the October-7 attack. More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, according to conservative estimates.

Like many others at the symposium, van Praagh says she is increasingly losing faith in politicians. "Never Again" has become an empty phrase, she argues, with little relevance to the everyday lives of Jews in Europe.

Jewish communities now have to protect themselves behind high walls. Constant security measures restrict their daily lives, she explains. "That is not what we want. We want to live in freedom."

Rabbi Menachem Margolin, chairman of the European Jewish Association, is also calling on European political leaders to take greater responsibility. He says he is grateful for their support, without which Jewish life in Europe would hardly be possible.

However, laws designed to protect Jewish life are often not enforced in practice. Many officials hesitate to call antisemitism by its name as soon as doing so becomes politically inconvenient. "But Auschwitz did not begin with gas chambers. It began with words," he cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regina Sluszny joined the delegation visiting the Birkenau memorial. The Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp, built by Nazi Germany, became a symbol of the Holocaust. The Nazis murdered around 1.1 million people there, including approximately one million Jews. Most were killed here at Birkenau.

The delegation is gathered to commemorate the November Pogroms of November 9 and 10, 1938, when Nazis set synagogues on fire, ransacked Jewish businesses and homes and murdered Jews. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps.

Survivors like Regina are increasingly rare. Most Holocaust survivors have passed away. Regina survived because, in 1942, a family friend and his wife took her in when she was just two years old while her parents fled the Nazis with her two brothers and went into hiding.

For more than 40 years, she has been sharing her story with schoolchildren, doing her part to ensure that the Holocaust is never forgotten. For her, "Never Again" is a promise that must be kept. Otherwise, it becomes a lie.

It comes down to choices made for speed and science, as the two spacecraft flew by planets in the 1970s and 1980s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure."

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#699. Rose Byrne on What Lured Her to ‘The Good Daughter’ and Why That Complicated Ending Wraps the Series

The star and executive producer unpacks the thrilling Peacock mystery also starring Meghann Fahy and if what happens to the young girl at the center of it is fair.

[This story contains major spoilers from The Good Daughter finale.]

Rose Byrne keeps outdoing herself. Her explosive limited series The Good Daughter co-starring Meghann Fahy quickly became the top show on Peacock. Just last year, she grabbed a best actress Oscar nomination and won both the Golden Globe and Independent Spirits Award for If I Had Legs I’d Kick You — the film nobody saw coming. She also wrapped season two of her Apple TV comedy Platonic.

Even for an actress with a pedigree like Byrne’s spanning over 30 years, projects like The Good Daughter are rare opportunities, she shared last year while still filming in the Atlanta Metro area. “Sam is the sort of role written for a man,” the Australian actress confessed. “It’s very dominant, kind of self-possessed, and she has physical trauma. Like she has scars, and she has a history. She has all this rich stuff that’s not always the case with the female roles you read.” Related Stories Beyond the Book Karin Slaughter Said "Absolutely Not" to Adapting Her Novel 'The Good Daughter.' Then She Wrote the Whole Series TV 'The Good Daughter' Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock's Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller

It’s the kind of story that Byrne, who also serves as executive producer alongside fellow Aussie, Big Little Lies Emmy winner Bruna Papandrea, sees as bestselling author and fellow EP Karin Slaughter’s superpower. “She writes incredibly rich female characters who are complicated and complex, and not all good and not all bad, and who have a lot to work with,” Byrne continued.

For the first time ever, Slaughter, who has had other books grace the screen with Pieces of Her for Netflix and, of course, Will Trent for ABC, adapted her own work and served as showrunner. The psychological thriller revolves around estranged sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn who, as teens, suffer a brutal attack in response to their father Rusty’s (an excellent Brendan Gleeson) work as an attorney that has left them scarred. Partial blindness and a permanent limp serve as enduring physical reminders for Sam. Spared many of the physical scars, Charlie’s show up in other ways. And they both lost their beloved mother Gamma (an effective Olivia Williams).

As the older sister, Sam sacrificed herself to ensure Charlie would be hurt the least, but that act created emotional and physical distance between the two. Rusty’s failing health has brought Sam back home from New York City, where she is a patent lawyer, to Pikeville, Georgia. It’s his defense of Kelly Wilson (impressive newcomer Shayna Benardo), a special needs high school girl seemingly behind a horrific school shooting that killed the school’s principal and a freshman girl that keeps her there.

What seems like an open-and-shut case is anything but. Because Charlie witnessed part of the shooting and is also an attorney, the two women can’t avoid each other. Any degree of separation disappears in a small town, especially for a polarizing case like this one, so emotional landmines abound. As the mystery surrounding Kelly’s actions lingers, the attack that the sisters survived years before also figures more prominently, forcing both Sam and Charlie to tackle all they have left unsaid and unresolved.

“One of the pleasures of this is that I wrote everything from the perspective of two women. So much to probably Meghann and Rose’s dismay, one of them always has to be in every single scene, because we get their perspective, and it’s a very internalized kind of storytelling,” Slaughter said on set. “But also, in a way, it shows their growth as sisters and as daughters, and gives me an opportunity to frame something that happens every day in America, basically through these very personal stories of these sisters who have been victims of violence before.”

On set when speaking to The Hollywood Reporter, Byrne noted “it’s rare you get to work side by side with a fellow actress.” That female energy is also directly sustained behind the camera with Oscar and Emmy-nominated director Steph Green (New Boy, Duster, Watchmen) and Australian cinematographer Zoë White (The Handmaid’s Tale). Below, she probes beyond the many plot twists to delve into aspects of the series that move her professionally and emotionally. Of course, we asked if there would be more and if she felt what happens to Kelly, the young girl at the center of the mystery, is fair.

In addition to playing Sam, you’re also an executive producer. What made you want to take on roles in front and behind the camera?

Being an EP was really like more of a seat at the table, particularly with casting. Getting Meghann Fahy on board was a huge deal for us. She’s so effervescent as Charlie; so magnetic and funny and heartbreaking. You just believe her straight away. She jumps. She lights up the screen, and she’s just gorgeous. I adore her. She’s so extraordinary, so talented.

And then Brendan Gleeson, who’s a legend at this point — so extraordinary and such a gifted storyteller — and so magnanimous with his work. I’ve known him since I was 23 when I did Troy. So that was a great thread. I worked with his son Domhnall Gleeson, so it was a lovely full circle to then have him playing my father. And that’s a tough character; it’s very polarizing. There’s a lot of fury that my character has at her father, a lot of anger and disappointment, and Brendan makes that hard because he’s so charming, but that’s what makes it interesting.

Reading the screenplay and the novel… it’s a classic origin story for Sam, where going back to where she came from, she’s dealing with all of her truths and all of the lies, and trying to uncover the past through this case; understanding her father more, but it felt to me almost a role written for a man, not particularly something you would see necessarily for a female character. That really intrigued me.

How did you pull off Sam’s physical transformation to convey her disability or disabilities?

Well, she has dysarthria, [her] speech disability from her trauma, and so I worked with my voice coach Kate Wilson, who’s extraordinary. She’s the head of voice [and speech] at Juilliard. I’ve worked with her for years and she’s incredible. She’s the most alive, passionate, compassionate teacher, and she’s really very sage. She and I delved in with what that would sound like, listening to tapes and recordings, and also working on the accent of Georgia and how my character had lived in New York for 20 years, and what it would sound like returning, and when it would return, and in what situations. When I return to Australia, my accent becomes a lot broader, and you know how you’re influenced by your environment.

Then with the limp, I worked with this wonderful PT trainer who works in rehab with people who’ve suffered injuries and so on. We homed in on what her limp would look like, and then did a million videos and would send them to Steph and figure out how far to go with it because we didn’t want it ever to be comical. Sometimes what reads on screen is very different in real life.

The younger Charlie [Drew Ann Cheek] and Sam [Audrey Grace Marshall] really match the older Charlie and Sam.

I was very front seat with the casting of that, so there was a lot of weighing in with everybody about who we felt the best lead was and, also, physically you have to have a lot of resemblance to them. I thought the girls were so wonderful, and that’s again a very hard job to do. I thought they just captured both Meghann and myself in really specific ways, and we watched a lot of footage of them as well. With Sam, obviously there’s a real before and after physically with what she goes through, so that was something I had to separately have work on. But establishing them as young women was so important.

While Sam and Charlie, in particular, experience extraordinary circumstances, the series seems to center on this whole idea of women holding onto very traumatic events or violations but still functioning in their lives.

Which we do every day. If you read the statistics about it, like one in six women have been sexually assaulted. A lot of people in America have suffered gun violence in their families. These statistics are horrific, and we worked very closely with RAINN who work with survivors of rape and incest and other horrific things, and they were incredible. We always had resources on set if people were being triggered or needed to talk. It was a safe space.

To Steph Green, our director, my first question was: “How will this be portrayed? I’m not interested in anything gratuitous or exploitative.” And Steph was so determined to tell the story in a way that had none of those tonal qualities in it. So absolutely the story has elements of trauma, but it’s dealt with in a very delicate way that I think is powerful but never gratuitous or exploitative.

Speaking of Steph, the way she, and Zoë White the cinematographer, handle the traumatic flashbacks is such an innovative technique that I don’t think I’ve seen.

I agree. I remember her telling me about that, how she was going to focus on hands and this and moments and shoot close-ups of various things to sort of link the story. And it’s beautifully told. The sense of memory was really vivid, I felt, [in] a lot of those flashbacks to me. I feel like they achieved something quite innovative.

When Rusty dies, everything is understandably sad. But the coffin scene at the funeral home manages to be both light and heavy. Did it come at a time when you guys kind of needed a break?

Meghann was so heartbreaking in that scene, and she’s so funny, too. That was actually great because what was harder was the flashback scene when we’re in New York, and it precipitates the estrangement. That scene was a lot harder because we’re through a closed door, sort of screaming a monologue and it’s a flashback, and I’ve got a wig on. That to me was more of a leap of faith. I think that was a harder needle to thread. Whereas the coffin scene, as you called it, was so gratifying to be able to look at her and really have a scene like two actors opposite one another and have such rich material. It was definitely strange for Brendan because he was in the coffin for a little bit. That’s no fun. But that was a scene I was both scared and excited to do.

There are so many powerful scenes, what are some of your favorite moments, or what stands out most to you?

The scene that haunts me so much is when Charlie confronts Judith over the kitchen table. I remember reading it in the novel, and I remember the first one I read in the screenplay, and my hair on my body was just standing on end. It was so suspenseful, so tightly drawn, and the history alone between these two women across each other from this table to then reach this boiling point of this scene was just masterful storytelling.

And it’s interesting because Sam and Charlie don’t have that traumatic relationship with them that Kelly has. Then considering that she’s special needs. So it’s unfathomable that the Pinkmans could do something like this to Kelly, right?

Yeah Karin, she’s a master storyteller, and just when you think you know where something is going. I found myself reading the novel and reading the screenplay [drawn to] the turns of what these people do and the perspectives that she puts on each situation. But that scene still haunts me.

I think it’s a very, very complicated answer and question. It’s such a nuanced and complicated story that has led her to this horrific situation that we made her in at the beginning. I really was fascinated with the process of that. I spoke to many lawyers who work in the criminal justice system about the process and how it works, and where you end up, and how you interrogate a witness, and like the defense team, and all of that. And Karin so beautifully captures how hard that system is and how it fails again and again and again for people, but how also you can have some wins. But it’s very nuanced and it’s very complicated.

It was a learning curve for me to even begin to understand that. So I think [Karin] has such a great understanding of that, and also the genre of a thriller, you know, and creating the suspense of that. Right until the very last episode, you’re really on the edge of your seat, as she just twists and turns and uses the perspective of one character then the other, and you constantly have shifting alliances, and she’s just very unflinching in her portrait of things. And that’s brave.

That’s why I ask if what happens to Kelly is fair because it’s very clear in the end how manipulated she was. And given her mental capacity, she wasn’t really aware of what she was doing.

Do you see a continuation to The Good Daughter?

I don’t. It feels contained to this series, like the novel, to me. I have hope for the characters that they would, I mean, selfishly, continue to have a better relationship with one another after all the trauma and all the things they’ve weathered or the storms they’ve weathered. But it felt, to me, pretty contained about this specific thing they had to go through.

I’m sure you take lessons from each project that you do. What is your biggest takeaway from this one?

I think diving back into this genre was really interesting for me [because] I hadn’t done it for many years. [There are] tropes that are really fun in there, and the challenges of a very complicated plot at times, and being ahead of it for myself. But Karin, the author, is really ahead of everybody. So, it was interesting. Also to work with an author who then wrote the screenplay, that was also something I’d never done creatively, and how fun that was. Also, we would have rigorous conversations where we would disagree about things, and that was fun too. I think I learned a lot.

All six episodes of The Good Daughter are streaming on Peacock.

#696. ‘Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ EPs on How ‘Orange County’ Became the First Franchise Extension, Season 2 Hopes and “Exploring” More Spinoffs

Jeff Jenkins and Lisa Filipelli speak with THR about expanding the ‘Mormon Wives’ franchise, what spinoffs they hope to pursue in the future and how the cast set OC's first season up for success.

Hulu’s first extension of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives franchise arrived on the streamer last Thursday, introducing viewers to a brand-new pool of women based in Southern California who are in some way connected to the LDS faith.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County has caused a stir online, proving that the format of the original series works with the franchise treatment. The online buzz has translated into viewership: season one accumulated 20 million hours in its first five days of streaming, a 12 percent increase over season five of the original series. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Couples Perform Double Dances as Another Top-Scoring Duo Exits Before Season 35 Finale: See the Scores, Who Went Home TV 'The Traitors' Season 5 Sets Release Date as First Trailer Highlights "Chorus of Chaos" to Come

So, what actually is in the secret sauce in Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives format? Executive producers Jeff Jenkins and Lisa Filipelli both agree everything boils down to casting.

“A docuseries, in my opinion, is only as good as the folks who are the subject, who are on camera, right? So we just try really hard to collaborate with our cast members and bring their stories forward,” Jenkins says. “It just goes back to story and sharing. We look for subjects, castmembers, who are really ready to share. It’s not an easy thing to do.”

Most of the women, like the original show, have built a presence on social media before reality television cameras began capturing their lives. Among them are Aspyn Ovard, an original family channel YouTuber who is now in a throuple; Madison Bontempo, another family-style YouTuber who used to be close with the Paul brothers; and Bobbi Althoff, the podcaster behind those viral Drake and Lil Yachty interviews.

Jen Affleck, of course, hails from the original Utah-based Mormon Wives series, while Avery Woods and Salomé Andrea also have large platforms online; Ashleigh Pease, Jordan McClanahan and McCall Dapron did not have massive social media careers pre-Hulu, leaving them as hidden gems who bring more insight into the religious perspective of the what secret life of a Mormon wife can look like without content creation.

Ovard opened up about her daughter’s terminal cancer diagnosis in season one, marking one of the most vulnerable admissions across the Mormon Wives franchise. When navigating how to share her story, Jenkins says, “It’s up to Aspyn to share what she wants to share, especially with the very delicate situations that she’s living in and through.”

“We don’t direct the ladies of this show or any other show that [Jeff Jenkins Productions] is producing on what to share and what to hold back. That is their decision, but they understand if they’re working with us, collaborating together, that the more you share, the more powerful the experience is going to be for the viewer,” Jenkins says, while also citing Pease opening up about the abuse she experienced in her childhood as another moving story from season one of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

The executive producer says he was “knocked on the floor by [Pease’s] resilience and her ability to overcome and build a life that she could only dream of when she was growing up.” Jenkins also commends DaPron and McClanahan’s strong ties to their faith, while noting he found Althoff opening up about her social anxiety to be “relatable to so many younger people who experience social anxiety or awkwardness.”

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County was initially critiqued when announced due to the name of the show; fans believed most of the cast were not Mormon. Castmembers DaPron and McClanahan also repeatedly highlighted during season one that they were on a show about Mormon wives, with the title itself bleeding into the dynamics amongst the cast.

“I think what’s so interesting for so many people who grow up in religious households is, even if you are not practicing, it impacts the way that you live every single day,” Filipelli says. “Everyone in this cast has been touched by the faith. And so I think the title, it is what it is. But I think the story from the show and the experience that these women have is so valid and informs who they are as adults, as mothers, as wives today.”

There could be an argument that Hulu could have expanded the franchise merely as Secret Lives, to make room for a different group of religious wives (e.g. The Secret Lives of Catholic Wives).

But Jenkins says there’s something so “mysterious” about the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints that lends itself well to the show where “we’re all learning about it together.”

Hulu also revealed in its reported viewership numbers that The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives franchise as a whole has driven over half a billion hours globally. That would mean continuing to expand the franchise into its own universe, similar to Bravo’s Real Housewives, would likely be imminent.

Jenkins says they’re “always exploring opportunities for new series, new ‘spinoffs,’ quote unquote.” Although it ultimately comes down to “if there are other groups of women out there who have compelling stories.”

Jenkins assures there are “other cities in America and different states in America that do have significant populations of folks who are following the Mormon faith.”

He also teases a potential international aspect of the Mormon religion: “There’s also an international aspect to this faith in Europe and in some of the other countries that are English-speaking. So, Lisa and I and Hulu, we’re all exploring.”

“If we can find another city with another great group that wants to share, and it’s somehow a shade different from Utah and different from OC, heck yeah!” Jenkins offers.

As for the future of Mormon Wives: Orange County, he jokes, “As far as production and producers, we’re ready to pick cameras back up tomorrow.”

“Go ask Hulu!” Filipelli says with a laugh as Jenkins adds, “We need a greenlight from Hulu.”

Season one of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County is available to stream on Hulu.

It now takes 24 hours for even a single particle of light to reach Voyager.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.

"The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance."

The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond.

On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn.

"Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries.

"And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she added. "So it's one of the only moons that has a thick atmosphere."

Decades later, Voyager 1's data is still incredibly important for scientists studying the planets and moons of our cosmic neighborhood. Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa. And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager.

"Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said. "I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper. Voyager is right there at the top of the list. And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have. So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later."

Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. On Aug. 25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system. After crossing that boundary, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space and has been exploring the interstellar medium ever since. Voyager 2 followed suit in November 2018.

While the Voyager spacecraft have left the heliosphere, they have technically not left the solar system, as they are still within the gravitational influence of the sun. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history.

The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return.

"You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back."

That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong.

"It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could."

As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory.

"Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said.

So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space.

"Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there."

How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges?

"Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said.

Spilker is a longtimeVoyager veteran. Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission. After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today.

"I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said.

The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker. But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers.

"Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared. "We have someone whose parents weren't born when Voyager was launched, and then we just celebrated the 90th birthday of one of the members who retired and came back. He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager."

Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager. Another big milestone is just ahead, when the mission turns 50 this upcoming year. And Spilker is optimistic that this will not be the end.

"I see the 50th anniversary as just a milestone," Spilker said. "The next milestone, and then we'll just keep on going."

As Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, you might wonder whenVoyager 2 will hit the same milestone. Since Voyager 2 is on a slower trajectory,it won't reach one light-day from Earth until 2035, nearly a decade into the future. The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #694. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

#693. Bear Grylls, Dhar Mann, Erin Foster, Lonnie Ali, Cameron Alexander and Sonja Warfield to Be Honored at Variety’s Third Annual Faith & Spirituality in Entertainment Honors

Rainn Wilson will host the evening presented by the Coalition for Faith & Media on Dec. 2.

Variety has announced its Faith and Spirituality in Entertainment Visionary Awards honorees who will be recognized at the third annual Faith and Spirituality in Entertainment Honors, presented by the Coalition for Faith & Media in Los Angeles, on Dec. 2.

The Honors will celebrate individuals who are supporting often underrepresented themes of faith and spirituality across film and TV. The event coincides with Variety’s annual Faith & Media Impact Report, recognizing those who are championing belief-centered storytelling within the entertainment industry. Related Stories ‘Drummer Boy’ Review: Love, Family and Revolution Conflict at Musket’s Point in a Swoony Period Musical

The honorees for the evening include: Bear Grylls, two-time Emmy Award-winner and best-selling author; Dhar Mann, founder Dhar Mann Studios; Erin Foster, creator, “Nobody Wants This”; Lonnie Ali, executive producer of Muhammad Ali TV series “The Greatest”; Cameron Alexander, screenwriter, “Heart of the Beast”; and Sonja Warfield, the Emmy-nominated co-showrunner and executive producer for HBO’s highly awarded drama, “The Gilded Age.”

Grylls is a former British Special Forces soldier, who became one of the youngest climbers to summit Mount Everest. He went on to host a string of hit adventure series, including Discovery Channel’s “Man vs. Wild” and “Running Wild With Bear Grylls,” now in its ninth season.

Foster is a writer, actress, and producer best known for creating the acclaimed comedy series “Nobody Wants This,” an AFI Awards honoree nominated for Golden Globe, Emmy, and Critics Choice Awards. Under her Fatigue Sisters overall deal with 20th Television, she is currently developing the drama “These Summer Storms,” based on Sarah MacLean’s novel, for Hulu. Beyond television, Erin co-owns the fashion brand Favorite Daughter and co-hosts the award-winning “The World’s First Podcast.”

Mann is an influential storyteller and founder of Dhar Mann Studios, an audience-first global entertainment company dedicated to uplifting audiences through stories and experiences that help people feel seen and connected. The studio reaches more than 170 million followers and generates over 320 million views each week across platforms.

Ali is an executive producer on the upcoming Amazon biopic series “The Greatest” and the documentary, “The City of Ali.” She is also the creator and co-host of the award-winning podcast “Ali in Me” on Audible and will executive produce a planned documentary about the relationship between Muhammad Ali and legendary broadcaster Howard Cosell. She and her husband opened the Muhammad Ali Center in Louisville in November of 2005, where she serves as a lifetime director and vice chair of the board. The Muhammad Ali Center’s mission is to inspire greatness, cultivate curious and courageous leaders, and grow a more compassionate world.

Cameron’s original feature screenplay, “Heart of the Beast,” is a survival thriller film starring Brad Pitt that was released in September this year. He recently wrote “Dreams in Antlered Moonlight,” which he will direct in his feature directorial debut.

Warfield is a television writer, producer and author whose credits include her work on the Emmy Award-winning NBC sitcom “Will & Grace” as well as BET’s hit comedy “The Game.” Currently, she’s the Emmy-nominated executive producer and co-showrunner for HBO’s highly awarded drama, “The Gilded Age.”

The night will feature award presentations to the honorees, alongside a networking reception and seated dinner, hosted by Rainn Wilson.

Wilson is the Emmy-nominated and SAG award-winning actor best known for playing Dwight Schrute for nine seasons on “The Office.” He is also a New York Times best-selling author, whose latest book is entitled “The Soul Boom Workbook: Spiritual Tools for Modern Living.” He co-founded the digital media company SoulPancake and Lide Haiti, an arts and education non-profit in rural Haiti.

“We are honored to partner with the Coalition for Faith & Media and Fetzer Institute to advance a meaningful conversation about the portrayal of faith and spirituality in media,” said Dea Lawrence, co-president and publisher of Variety. “Media plays a powerful role in shaping cultural understanding and influencing how we see one another. Creating greater awareness of the diverse ways faith and spirituality inform people’s lives is essential to fostering more authentic, nuanced and inclusive storytelling.”

“More than three-quarters of the world identifies as religious, spiritual, or a person of faith,” said Brooke Zaugg, executive director, Coalition for Faith and Media. “Audiences want to see their values reflected in the stories they watch. It’s good business and a meaningful way to create greater understanding of those around us. We’re grateful for Variety’s leadership, honoring the diverse industry voices who are bringing faith to the screen in artful, nuanced, and entertaining ways.”

Past honorees have included Mo Amer, Tiffany Haddish, Viola Davis, Sheryl Lee Ralph, Jay Shetty, and Julius Tennon.

Thermal satellites from an Indian startup aim to spot urban heat, crop stress and wildfires from orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology.

Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany.

The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said.

SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs, too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said.

SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2.

The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up.

Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave.

TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team.

Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad.

A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said.

Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year."

He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy."

The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said.

SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit, is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations.

"There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul, are flying regularly, "things will be much easier."

SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade.

Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build.

"If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#690. Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military

Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.

Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee. According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known.

"The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue.

"There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. The Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are statistically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Around 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment.

For physical harassment, 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct, and 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was not wanting to draw attention to themselves.

"There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism.

Defense policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfill their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction.

"Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defense Minister Pistorius stressed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defense must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr urgently needs additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

This article was originally written in German.

#689. As U.S. Infrastructure Crumbles, ABC’s ‘World News Tonight’ Posts Highest Week-Long Daily Ratings Since COVID

A week after the midterm elections generated tremendous audiences for the network evening newscasts, last week’s unpredictable string of news — including the Microsoft Outlook blackout, followed by the nationwide grounding of air flights — propelled ABC’s “World News Tonight” to heights the telecast hasn’t seen in years.

The busy news week also included the Nvidia scandal, the Brooklyn building collapse, the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, fallout from the midterm elections (and late-breaking results like Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom) and more. Related Stories ‘Drummer Boy’ Review: Love, Family and Revolution Conflict at Musket’s Point in a Swoony Period Musical

According to ABC News, “World News Tonight” averaged more than 9 million Total Viewers on each of its five telecasts last week — the first time it has done that in nearly six years, during the COVID era (specifically, the week of Feb. 15, 2021).

“Audiences are turning to ‘World News Tonight with David Muir’ in numbers we haven’t seen since the COVID pandemic, a powerful reflection of the trust they place in our journalism during uncertain times,” said ABC News president Almin Karamehmedovic in a statement to Variety. “Amid a relentless week of breaking news, culminating in Friday’s nationwide ground stop, more than 9 million Americans tuned in every single night. We are deeply grateful for their confidence and never take that responsibility for granted.”

Over the entire week (except for Monday, which wasn’t included due to Monday Night Football), “World News Tonight with David Muir” was No. 1 with total viewers (9.251 million) on all of broadcast and cable (excluding sports) for the second week in a row and landed its best number in four years, according to Nielsen’s Live+Same Day Big Data Plus Panel Program Ratings.“World News Tonight with David Muir” was also No. 1 with adults 25-54 (1.366 million) and adults 18-49 (993,000). In comparison, “NBC Nightly News” averaged 7.117 million total viewers, 1.161 million with adults 25-54 and 849,000 with adults 18-49, while “CBS Evening News” averaged 4.633 million viewers, 689,000 with adults 25-54 and 527,000 among adults 18-49.

Season to date, “World News Tonight” is up 14% year-to-year in total viewers (8.679 million vs. 7.586 million), up 34% with adults 25-54 (1.214 million vs. 907,000) and up 40% with adults 18-49 (883,000 vs. 629,000), based on Most Current Big Data+Panel Ratings. ABC notes that “World News Tonight” is posting its best ratings since the 2020-2021 season and that its total viewers lead over “NBC Nightly News” is its largest advantage in 32 years, and its lead over “CBS Evening News” is its largest advantage in at least 35 years.
