#648. What Is the Moon Base?

NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore.

______________________________________________________________________

outpost: a station or base located in a remote, distant place

infrastructure: the basic framework and systems that make up a larger building or organization

terrain: the physical features, shape, and layout of the surface of a piece of land, including its slope and elevation

regolith: the layer of loose, fragmented rock and mineral dust covering most of the lunar surface

______________________________________________________________________

The Moon Base will be built in the lunar South Pole region. This area was selected for its unique lighting conditions and potential for scientific discovery.

Near the lunar South Pole, the Sun stays low on the horizon. Some areas can receive extended periods of sunlight. Other areas stay in shadows for long periods of time. In some craters, sunlight may never reach the surface at all.

Areas that receive extended sunlight could be good for generating solar power. Longer sunlight hours are also good for navigating and exploring. Areas that remain in shadows are some of the coldest areas on the Moon. In these locations, scientists hope to find deposits of frozen water ice.

The Moon Base will be constructed in three phases. Each phase will build on what is learned along the way.

Phase One is taking place right now. Over the next few years, NASA and its partners will send robotic missions to explore the lunar South Pole region. They will test new technologies and practice landing on the Moon. This phase will include multiple different landers and lunar terrain vehicles. These missions will conduct science experiments and look for the best locations for building the Moon Base.

Phase Two is planned for 2029-2032. During this period, NASA will begin setting up long-term infrastructure. This includes things like power systems, cargo transportation, and communications hardware. These components will be set up across multiple locations. This will allow for future expansion of the Moon Base.

During Phase Three, NASA will begin assembling a permanent lunar outpost. This is where astronauts will be able to live and work for extended periods. Habitats, power and communication systems, and transportation will all come together to grow Moon Base.

Crewed and robotic lunar rovers will play an important role in the development of the Moon Base. These rovers will test out technologies, transport astronauts, map terrain, and more. Let’s learn about a few of the rovers being built as part of the Moon Base.

NASA’s VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) is fully built. It is being tested at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In 2027, it will launch to the Moon from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its mission will be to explore permanently shadowed craters to look for water and other resources. It will travel more than 15 miles, collecting data and analyzing the lunar soil.

NASA’s PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) is a nuclear-powered rover. It is being built from existing hardware that was created for NASA’s Mars rover missions. PROMISE will look for resources – like potential water ice – on and below the lunar surface. It will carry multiple science instruments, including several that are also on VIPER. The mission is targeted to launch by late 2028.

Lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs) will launch to the lunar South Pole region by 2028. These crewed vehicles will be driven by astronauts during missions to the Moon. This will allow the crew to explore larger areas and gather geology samples. When astronauts are not on the Moon, the LTVs will be remotely operated from Earth. They will map the lunar surface and collect data about the extreme environment in the region.

In addition to rovers, NASA’s MoonFall mission will send a group of propulsive drones to the Moon. They will land near the lunar South Pole by 2028. The drones will descend to the lunar surface independently. They will operate separately over the course of a single lunar day (about 14 Earth days). They will use high-definition cameras to map hard-to-reach terrain. This data will help NASA select potential Artemis landing sites.

The lunar South Pole region is an extreme environment. The Moon doesn’t have any noticeable atmosphere. This means temperatures can reach more than 130°F (54°C) in sunlit areas. And it can be as cold as -334°F (-203°C) inside permanently shadowed craters. This can be very dangerous for astronauts. But it is also a challenge for designing infrastructure and hardware.

Navigating the uneven lunar surface can be difficult. The South Pole region of the Moon has steep slopes, ridges, rocks, and deep craters. Shackleton Crater is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. Detailed mapping and robotic exploration will help NASA identify safe landing areas and plan routes for astronauts and rovers.

The lunar surface is covered with regolith. This layer of rocky material is the result of meteoroid impacts. Since there is no wind or rain to cause erosion on the lunar surface, regolith particles have sharp edges. This means regolith can quickly wear down spacesuits and equipment. It can be particularly irritating to skin and dangerous if inhaled. Precautions must be taken to keep regolith and lunar dust out of areas where astronauts live.

The Moon Base is an important step in learning how to live and work on another world. What we learn on the lunar surface by testing new landing techniques, construction methods, and exploration technologies will help prepare for human missions to Mars.

Here are a few examples of the careers that are making NASA’s Moon Base plans possible:

Space tire engineer: The rovers being designed as part of the Moon Base need to have special tires. Engineers must consider the lack of atmosphere, extreme temperature, and rocky terrain when designing tires to drive long distances on the Moon. A career in engineering demands a strong understanding of math and complex problem-solving. An advanced college degree is usually required. Click here to see a space tire engineer in action.

Exploration geologist: These scientists study rocks and minerals on Earth and throughout the solar system. They look at geological processes to see how erosion and harsh environments can change terrain. For Moon Base, they’re helping to select locations to explore on the lunar surface. And they’re helping train the astronauts who will land and gather samples. This career requires strong observational skills and usually requires an advanced college degree. Click here to see what it’s like being an exploration geologist at NASA.

Manufacturing technician: Turning designs into reality takes skilled technicians. Fabrication and assembly of robotic equipment and spacecraft parts requires precise calculations. Being able to follow intricate instructions is key. Trade school training and skills such as operating forklifts and heavy machinery may be required.

Instrument technician: These experts install, calibrate, and maintain sensors and control systems. They troubleshoot issues that might come up with delicate systems and equipment. This career path often starts with an apprenticeship or hands-on training alongside experienced technicians. An associate’s degree is often required. Click here to see some of the testing completed on one of the Moon Base landers.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#647. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

#646. Pokémon GO and Duolingo just launched a collab: How to unlock free Pikachu suits and Shiny encounters

TL;DR: Pokémon GO and Duolingo just teamed up for exclusive cross-app rewards. Score free Duolingo avatar suits, regional and shiny encounters, and more.

Pokémon GO and Duolingo just merged forces in one of the most delightfully chaotic app crossovers of the year.

Live from Nov. 17, the two mobile giants are running a cross-app event called Duo’s Pokémon Party. By keeping a seven-day language streak alive in Duolingo, players can unlock custom Pokémon outfits for their Duolingo avatars alongside a unique promo code for event-themed Timed Research in Pokémon GO.

To join, trainers must opt into Duo’s Pokémon Party inside the Duolingo app by Dec. 21, and finish at least one lesson per day across seven separate days before Dec. 29. It's that easy.

Maybe we're cynical, but this feels like a rare opportunity. It's refreshing to see a free cross-promotion that rewards daily habits across both platforms:

Four free Duolingo avatar suits: Completing daily lessons unlocks up to nine total rewards, headlined by four wearable Pokémon suits for your Duolingo profile: Pikachu, Chatot, a Poké Ball, and a Pokémon GO trainer outfit.

Regional and Shiny encounters in Pokémon GO: Finishing seven days of lessons generates a unique offer code redeemable on the Pokémon GO Web Store. That unlocks Timed Research featuring XP, Stardust, and guaranteed encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Lucario, and regional-exclusive Chatot.

Foreign-language gameplay and new language tags: When you activate the Timed Research, you pick a target language, and your tasks actually appear in that language. Caught Pokémon also debut a new Language Tag on their summary screen, letting you tap to inspect their official names across different languages.

We should note that while the Pokémon GO encounters are permanent additions to your Pokédex, the four Pokémon avatar suits are temporary rentals. All earned Pokémon suits will automatically expire and vanish from your Duolingo closet on March 31, 2027.

#645. What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

#644. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

Materials provided by Florida Museum of Natural History. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The Empire State Building is seen illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft as it was about to pass one light-day away from Earth, a distance reached by no other human-made object, Nov. 17, 2026. The color gold represents the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager; the Golden Record contains sounds and images selected to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#642. Xiaomi 18 Pro hands-on: Undeniably cool, incredibly powerful

What if your phone had a second display on the back?

If you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the new foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. The display is very cool and does bring some functionality that you otherwise just cannot have, though it's not nearly as versatile as what you get with a foldable phone.

I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like. The display on the back is what makes them stand out from the crowd, at least visually, but it's not something that will drastically change the way you use your phone.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is not Xiaomi's first phone to feature a secondary display on the back; last year's Xiaomi 17 Pro had one, too. Just like the main display on the front, it hasn't changed much since last year: It's still a 2.9-inch, 596x976 pixel AMOLED display, though it is a little brighter than before. I didn't get to try the 17 Pro, though, so the display on the back is new to me.

Displays: 6.9-inch, 1,208x2,624 pixel, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness; secondary display on the back: 2.9-inch, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness

Design: Dragon Crystal Glass 3 front, aluminum frame,

Size and weight: 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm; weight: 240 grams

Rear cameras: A triple rear camera system with a 200-megapixel, f/1.7 wide camera, a 200-megapixel, f/2.4 periscope telephoto camera, and a 50-megapixel, f/2.4 ultrawide camera

Front cameras: 50-megapixel, f/2.2 selfie camera

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB with 12/16GB of RAM

Battery life: 7,050mAh battery with 100W charging, 50 wireless, and 27W reverse wireless charging

Special features: Under display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, stereo audio system with 3 speakers, 24-bit/192kHz hi-res audio support

Yes, this is an extremely powerful phone, even though it isn't technically Xiaomi's flagship (that's the Ultra series, which isn't out yet this year). You get the latest Snapdragon chip, a massive camera upgrade over last year's 50-megapixel system, and a humongous battery that charges very quickly.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro, which I also received for testing but have spent less time with, has a 6.4-inch display, a smaller battery, with the rest being mostly the same.

Xiaomi flagships in the numbered series follow the same philosophy: Make a phone that's very much like an iPhone, but stuff it with extremely powerful hardware for added value. It starts with the phones' names (18 Pro and 18 Pro Max), it's visible in parts of the design, and Xiaomi's HyperOS, which has been upgraded to version 4 here, can be set up to mirror iOS in almost every way.

This is not a bad thing. The Xiaomi 18 Pro is distinctive enough with its dual display that overall iPhone-likeness doesn't feel like you're having a cheap copy. And I don't mind the HyperOS software being a dead ringer for iOS, down to the near-identical Control Center (which, you guessed it, is called the Control Center on the Xiaomi as well).

Do I need a display on the back of the phone? Not really. It's useful for photos as it can give cues to the folks you're photographing, and it can take your selfies game to the next level as you can actually take selfies with the 200-megapixel main camera system. Other than that, it just looks cool.

But you do need to see it in real life to appreciate just how cool it is. It's an excellent, super-bright, pixel-dense AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. I set it up with an ocean wave animation that looks downright beautiful when I touch it. You can have AI-based apps on there, and even use it for simple games. It's so good that I kept consciously placing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max on its face when setting it on a table, just to appreciate the crispness of that mini display on the back.

But other than the camera tricks, it's still (surprise!) preferable to use the much larger front display for most tasks. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Up until a few years ago, battery capacities north of 5,000mAh were reserved for thick specialty phones focusing on battery life. But then a couple of battery breakthroughs (including silicon-carbon battery tech which Xiaomi is using here) made it to the mass market, and now Xiaomi can place an 7,050mAh battery in the regular-sized Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

The battery charges quickly on a fast charger and it lasts for at least two days. It's so good that I didn't have proper time to really test it as I only charged the phone twice in little under a week.

I don't think I've ever used a Xiaomi phone that was as quick and worked as smoothly as this one. Everything I touched opened instantly (including the fingerprint scanner which takes a tiny fraction of a second to analyze your digit and log you in). Playing with animated, AI-based and fancy perspective wallpapers did not punish me in terms of speed, as the phone kept operating incredibly smoothly.

Yes, it has the latest Snapdragon chip inside, but I guess Xiaomi also polished its HyperOS 4 to make it a little speedier than before.

As is customary for Xiaomi, HyperOS does have a maddening number of features and options, some of which are tucked away in some menu you wouldn't think of. But given the versatility of this phone, it's hard to blame them. One I set the phone up as I liked, the complexity of the Settings did not bother me.

We've gotten to a point in which Xiaomi can put two 200-megapixel cameras, and a two 50-megapixel ones on a phone that's not really their camera flagship.

Do we need so many megapixels? Possibly not, as evidenced in the fact that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max takes 12.5 megapixel photos by default, and you have to manually up the resolution to either 50 or 200 megapixels.

But the high megapixel count opens up interesting possibilities, such as zooming in at 12.8x without losing quality. The telephoto camera doubles as a macro camera that can go in really close (its minimum focusing distance is 12 centimetres), with Xiaomi calling it a "telescope and microscope in one."

I haven't had enough time with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera to fully assess how good it is. From what I've seen, though, it's an incredibly versatile and powerful system that you can use to squeeze out a good photo in almost every scenario.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at 1,399 EUR, while the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at 1,599 EUR in Europe. The colors on offer are Cosmic Blue, Black, White, and Velvet Red for both devices. We don't have the exact date of availability yet, and will update this article when we get them.

Want more tech and digital culture news delivered to your inbox daily or sent straight to your device? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts.

Stan is a Senior Editor at Mashable, where he has worked since 2007. He's got more battery-powered gadgets and band t-shirts than you. He writes about the next groundbreaking thing. Typically, this is a phone, a coin, or a car. His ultimate goal is to know something about everything.
