#618. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

#617. A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life

To build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced new scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

To help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries

By highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the new approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," says SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically."

Materials provided by Staatliche Naturwissenschaftliche Sammlungen Bayerns. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#616. The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026

Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a big reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.

“We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”

Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.

The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.

The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable.

Something we missed? Let us know in the comments.

“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.

Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”

There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.

None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their new, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.

What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

#614. Rivian CEO says new R2 SUV, autonomy make 2027 an ‘inflection year’ as EV maker marks five years since IPO

It's been five years since Rivian Automotive celebrated its initial public offering with CEO and founder RJ Scaringe ringing the Nasdaq opening bell from the company's factory in Normal, Illinois, while the company's sleek vehicles sat outside the stock exchange in Times Square.

It was a euphoric time for all-electric vehicle companies that has since diminished. And much like the EV hype, Rivian's stock price is down more than 80% since the Amazon-backed company debuted on the Nasdaq at $78 per share on Nov. 10, 2021. That includes a nearly 30% decline this year.

A host of internal and external factors have contributed to Rivian's stock decline, but the company continues to be the most promising EV maker to emerge during the early 2020s, as most of its peer group to go public during that time no longer exists.

Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe acknowledges that not everything has gone to plan amid supply chain shortages, geopolitical tensions and slower-than-expected consumer EV adoption, but he said he believes the next year will prove to be a catalyst for the company and investors.

"2027 is really an inflection year for us," Scaringe told CNBC during an exclusive interview. "I'm excited to start to really show what we believe so fully, the potential of the business."

Scaringe's bullishness comes as Rivian ramps up production of its midsize R2 SUV — meant to expand the brand to the mainstream market — and as the company continues to invest in its next generation of vehicle software and autonomy.

Scaringe said the R2, with an entry-level model at about $45,000, remains the core business to be able to showcase its newest technologies. Rivian delivered a record 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, up 46% year over year, and said R2 was already its best-selling vehicle by volume, outselling both its R1 flagship products and its commercial van.

"That's going to define the business. The path to profitability, the path to very significant growth in revenue is all built around R2, and then some of the variants that come following R2," Scaringe said.

For the most recent period, Rivian said the automotive cost of goods sold per vehicle improved by more than $12,000 quarter over quarter, helped by a higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage.

Rivian also is in the midst of building a new multibillion-dollar Georgia factory that Scaringe has said is necessary to get the company to the volumes it needs to achieve net profitability.

Its sole factory in Normal, Illinois, is capable of producing 215,000 vehicles annually. That includes up to 155,000 R2s alongside R1 models and electric vans. Rivian said the Georgia plant will be capable of producing up to 300,000 units annually once the initial phase construction is completed in late 2028.

Of course, all of that means additional capital spending and pressure on the company to improve profits.

"We've made the decision to simultaneously work towards profitability … and deeply invest in our technology, and in particular in autonomy," Scaringe said.

Rivian's operating performance is improving, but several Wall Street analysts expect the company's investment requirements to rise significantly in 2027.

Rivian generated $176 million of consolidated gross profit in the third quarter, but its automotive business posted an $80 million gross loss, while its software and services unit generated $256 million of gross profit at a 42% margin.

Wall Street analysts broadly agree Rivian's R2 launch is showing encouraging early demand and lowering manufacturing costs, but they're concerned about whether that can offset rising autonomy spending, the Georgia factory buildout and continued cash burn.

"Funding has long been a key debate for Rivian investors," Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu said in an Oct. 30 investor note after the company reported quarterly results that exceeded Wall Street's expectations. "The notion of a multi-year (even if credible) path to cash flow breakeven will be less attractive to investors."

Rivian said during its late October earnings call that its total available future liquidity is expected to be about $13 billion when factoring in available credit and money from partnerships with Volkswagen and Uber as well as a $4.5 billion U.S. Department of Energy loan for the Georgia plant.

Rivian said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion to end the third quarter.

The company may still need to raise more capital. Scaringe said Rivian plans to be "opportunistic" about any additional capital raises, which have previously included equity deals with Volkswagen and Uber.

"As we think about the environment looking out, we want to continue to position ourselves to be in a place to invest in the technology. And so that means we'll be opportunistic as it pertains to capital. But I want to be clear: We're like very focused on getting the profitability," Scaringe said.

The company has significantly upgraded the software capabilities and hardware on its vehicles to prepare them for autonomy technologies, or physical artificial intelligence, as Scaringe calls it.

The next step in that is releasing "point-to-point" driving capabilities, in which the vehicles can drive on their own from destination to destination with the driver acting as a monitor in case of any unexpected problems.

U.S. EV leader Tesla is the only automaker to currently offer those features on its vehicles. Scaringe said Rivian plans to not only catch up to Tesla's capabilities but exceed them as it uses multiple sensor types to allow the vehicle to "see" better, especially in inclement weather.

"That's not like the finish line. ... Think of it as like the starting point where you suddenly have a more apples to apples comparison between Rivian and Tesla," Scaringe said.

The release of point-to-point over the coming weeks and months, first to employees and then to customers, is expected to be followed by autonomous vehicles with Uber by 2028.

Scaringe said he believes such technologies will become a differentiator for the company in the coming years.

"I think it will go from a purchase consideration for maybe 10% of the buying public that's in the top five things considered in making a purchase decision to the No. 1 or No. 2 purchase consideration for the vast majority of buyers," Scaringe said.

Rivian plans to offer more details about its AI and autonomous plans during a second annual investor technology event on Dec. 9.

"We view this as a likely positive catalyst as the event could set a path for AV features driving incremental vehicle demand & higher [software] revenue in 2027, building on 2026 growth," TD Cowen analyst Itay Michaeli said in an investor note last week.

Rivian's stock is currently rated overweight with a $17.70 target price, according to analyst estimates compiled by FactSet. That would be a roughly 26% increase from its Monday closing price but still a far cry from its IPO.

#613. Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. New research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to new threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

Using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved."

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to new challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," says Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state."

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with new challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society."

Materials provided by Universitat Pompeu Fabra - Barcelona. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#611. Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans

A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

#610. 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

New forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling new support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?"

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," said Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans."

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced."

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

The results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls showed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing important new evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

The researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

Additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal New Clues to Egypt's Dark Past

The findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve important clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" said Campbell. "Still, this study shows how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one."

#609. Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?

Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.

We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.

The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable.

Something we missed? Let us know in the comments.

Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.

Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.

And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.

Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.

There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.

Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.

Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.

Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.

At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.

Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

Yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.

Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

#608. Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers."

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful new way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

To investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

The results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss

The new scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people."

Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang said. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be."

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

Zhang recognized that this approach could overlook important biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he said. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns."

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

The Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

They examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

The comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas showed greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance

The team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

At the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores showed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, important differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

People whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao said. "Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves."

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements showed some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he said.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially shows a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

For example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

Importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he said. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies."

Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important new direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

With just days to go before Grand Theft Auto VI comes out, Xbox players might be wondering if they'll have to buy the game at all.

#606. Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus says the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.)

Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

At only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

The HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

There were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box said it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

Two, this device is not currently FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

#605. A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

The object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets currently recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

The discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

"Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World

The breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman quickly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

To check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

Because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

However, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

Rubin Observatory has an important advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

Even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 new trans-Neptunian objects.

The team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

Rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate new discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

"Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system."

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows users to explore its structure in real time.

Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

#604. Google commemorates Robert Pattinsons James Bond casting with a sneaky Easter egg

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond has left Google feeling shaken, not stirred.

Following the announcement that Pattinson would be our next 007, Google introduced a new Bond-themed Easter egg. If you search up Pattinson's name, the search results shake a little, and a small twist of lemon falls from the top of the screen to rest daintily on Pattinson's head.

The Easter egg is a nod to James Bond's classic cocktail order: a vodka martini, shaken, not stirred. Google has essentially turned Pattinson into the cocktail he'll be ordering onscreen.

Pattinson's casting as Bond came after weeks of speculation and reported screen tests for potential Bond candidates, including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, and Nicholas Hoult.

Pattinson will star in the as-yet unnamed 26th Bond film, the first since Daniel Craig took his last bow in 2021's No Time To Die. Dune helmer Denis Villeneuve is set to direct. The pair have also worked together on the upcoming Dune: Part Three. Villeneuve and Pattinson's Bond film does not yet have a release date.

Bond won't be the first franchise Pattinson has led to be commemorated with a Google Easter egg. In 2022, tied to The Batman's release, if you searched terms such as "Bruce Wayne" or "Gotham City," a yellow Bat-Signal would appear alongside the results. Clicking on it turned the page into a moody Gotham night, complete with thunder, the Bat-Signal, and Batman swinging around the screen.

Plus, if you search up "Twilight" now, you'll be treated to a small line of scrolling text that reads "hoa hoa hoa season," flanked by falling leaf emojis. The Easter egg references Twilight fans' loving nickname for fall, drawn from the so-called "hoa hoa hoa" vocals of Blue Foundation's "Eyes on Fire" from the Twilight soundtrack.
