#562. How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.

Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It's going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don't think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you're immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don't really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what's different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

#561. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease."

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," said Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see."

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

The results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies."

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," said Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies."

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," said Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment."

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal new treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

#560. Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion

BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

"It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell."

Keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase."

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also said the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

"The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through."

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

#559. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#557. Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies."

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research

The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur."

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

#556. A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto)

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio)

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati)

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota)

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders

Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

"These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders."

#554. Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang

As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO. And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back.

At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure.

“On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said.

Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.”

Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”

One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI.

Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago.

The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago.

Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee.

Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions.

On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation.

Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.”

However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week.

But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.”

Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon.

Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

#553. 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife. Researchers have uncovered ancient stone tools, fossils of large animals, and rare plant remains that offer an unusually detailed look at how early humans survived in this dramatically different environment.

The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region. Announced by the Saudi Heritage Commission, the findings are the result of a joint investigation involving the Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University. Published in Science, the research brings together specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, along with experts from several international institutions. Their work provides important new evidence about prehistoric human activity, environmental change, and early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife

Today, much of this region is dominated by desert, but the landscape looked very different during the last Interglacial period, around 125,000 years ago. This warm, humid chapter of Arabian history is often called Green Arabia, a time when plentiful water and vegetation supported large animals and human populations.

Using satellite-based terrain modeling, scientists reconstructed an enormous ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers. The lake reached depths of up to 29 meters. Evidence from sediments, the surrounding landscape, and the remains of aquatic organisms indicates that it was a relatively stable freshwater environment bordered by open grasslands and vegetation.

The researchers identified more than 500 plant and animal fossil specimens, including invertebrates, spread across more than 130 locations. Among the animals that once inhabited the area were hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. These discoveries reveal a rich prehistoric ecosystem that bears little resemblance to the dry landscape found there today.

Thousands of Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Human Ingenuity

Alongside the fossils, archaeologists recovered 5,511 stone tools measuring more than 2 centimeters from the main excavation area. More than 98% were made from flint, and analysis showed that the people who created them used Levallois techniques, a method of shaping stone to produce carefully prepared flakes.

To better understand how the tools were made and used, researchers conducted systematic surveys using a grid system to document and collect artifacts and fossils. They also applied two dating methods to sand and fossil teeth, used three-dimensional techniques to determine how stone fragments fit together, and examined tool surfaces with microscopic and chemical analyses.

These investigations uncovered intriguing evidence of how early humans used the plants around them. Residues preserved on stone tools included traces from several types of vegetation, some of which contain toxic compounds. Resin and woody material suggest that certain stone tips were attached to handles or shafts to make hunting weapons.

Other plant residues point to the processing of tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. This suggests that the people living around the lake relied on vegetation for a variety of purposes, from obtaining food to carrying out everyday activities.

Perhaps most surprisingly, the findings raise the possibility that prehistoric hunters incorporated poisonous plant compounds into their hunting technology. Although this interpretation remains tentative, it represents some of the earliest potential evidence of such practices identified in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region's earliest known evidence of palm-related vegetation.

A Rare Glimpse Into Everyday Life 125,000 Years Ago

What makes Uruq al-Julaybah especially valuable is the unusual combination of discoveries preserved at one location. The animal fossils, manufactured tools, and plant remains were all recovered from the same dated archaeological setting (animal remains, stone tools, and plant material), allowing scientists to piece together a remarkably complete picture of prehistoric life.

The shores of ancient Lake Mundafan appear to have provided an ideal gathering place for early humans. Freshwater, animals, vegetation, and materials suitable for making tools were all available in the surrounding landscape.

Evidence suggests that people used this environment for numerous activities, including manufacturing stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animals and plants, and working with plant fibers. Taken together, the discoveries indicate that these early populations were highly adaptable and made sophisticated use of the resources available to them.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a Heritage Commission researcher and professor of Paleolithic archaeology who participated in the project, emphasized the importance of the discovery at Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter. He described it as a significant archaeological find that helps explain how the ancient environment shaped the lives of humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia during early prehistory.

Reconstructing a Forgotten Chapter of Human History

"This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," said Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University's Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. "The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant."

By bringing together different kinds of archaeological and environmental evidence, the researchers have reconstructed a period of Arabian history that is difficult to imagine from the region's present-day appearance. Their findings offer important clues about how early humans moved across the Arabian Peninsula, developed technology, and adapted their behavior to changing environmental conditions.

"Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories," said Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

The investigation reflects an extensive international research effort to better understand the Arabian Peninsula's ancient human and environmental history. The Saudi Heritage Commission supported fieldwork during the 2023 season, helped fund the research, and facilitated scientific activities.

Along with KAUST, Griffith University in Australia, and King Saud University, the project involved international universities and research centers specializing in archaeology, ancient environments, history, and laboratory analysis. This collaboration demonstrates how combining expertise from different scientific fields can uncover extraordinary details about human life thousands of generations in the past.

#552. What's going on with the polar vortex?

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

#550. NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base

NASA has launched a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.

"We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next."

NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an important step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.

"As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay."

Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon

The competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.

Each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore new approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.

The challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.

Students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.

Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers

Beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.

"Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," said Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge

Interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.

NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

#549. Nvidia ends Jensen Huangs hopes for return as CEO

Nvidia held its Q3 2027 earnings call on Tuesday, less than a week after former CEO Jensen Huang resigned amidst reports he had engaged in multiple extramarital affairs — including with an alleged Chinese spy. While Huang did not appear during the earnings call, he did publish a statement saying that he would happily return to his former role as Nvidia's CEO if asked.

The AI boom has sparked a significant spike in demand for computer components, leading to increasing profits for chipmakers such as Nvidia. Earlier this year, the company reported $81.6 billion in revenue during Q1 and $96.2 billion in Q2. This growth has continued in Q4, with Nvidia announcing its quarterly revenue had increased by 20 percent to $115.8 billion.

However, the elephant in the room was Huang, whose recent scandal and departure prompted a significant drop in Nvidia's stock. During Tuesday's earnings call, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones stated that Huang had voluntarily resigned on Nov. 12 "after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms." Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO, with CFO Colette Kress acting in the role in the interim.

"The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," said Jones. "While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders."

Jones then shut down any further discussion regarding Huang's situation, stating that while Nvidia's board would issue further communications "when appropriate," it would not address or answer any questions about it during the earnings call.

"The board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward," said Jones.

Nvidia announced on Tuesday that it has established a committee to oversee its national security policies and export control compliance. The first of Huang's affair partners to be revealed was Alice Huang (no relation), a former Megaspeed executive accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent funnelling Nvidia chips to the country, which would be a violation of U.S. restrictions.

Interim CEO Kress also made efforts to reassure investors during Nvidia's earnings call, and stressed the value it places on its workers. Huang's second and third alleged affair partners were Nvidia employees, including its vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. Hours prior to Nvidia's earnings call, Huang took to X to issue his first public statement since stepping down as CEO last Thursday. In it, he expressed his appreciation for his friends and colleagues, reiterated his love for the U.S., and admitted he has made "mistakes."

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," said Huang. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret."

Huang further addressed calls for him to be reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, making it clear he would return if asked. The Financial Times previously reported that Huang had discussed reclaiming the role with people close to him, and was gathering other tech executives to lobby for his return.

It wouldn't be the first time a tech CEO reclaimed their role after being ousted. OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman in 2023, accusing him of lying, retaliating against critics, and creating a "toxic atmosphere." Altman was swiftly reinstated after days of outcry from supporters, with almost the entire board ultimately leaving instead.

Even so, judging by the Nvidia board's statements on Tuesday, Huang's hopes for a similar comeback are likely to remain mere hopes for now.

#548. Disney's 'Star Wars' is coming to Cosm domes ahead of 50th anniversary as part of multiyear film deal

On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology company announced a new studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration.

The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May.

"We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties."

This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The company is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December.

Each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment.

In this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor.

Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film.

"We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner."

The premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans.

Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies.

"What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice said. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business."

And Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise launches, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands.

#547. ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.

This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.

"Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022."

"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!"

Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids

Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.

With gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling quickly across the ground.

Rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an important safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.

Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids

Next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.

The mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.

Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

The mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.

Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision

Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.

The impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.

However, the experiment also raised important questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?

Researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.

These details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.

A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.

The spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.

Together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.
